# Rough ride on LL Bean Subaru, are the struts the cause?

There is a persistent myth in the automotive community that suspension components remain functional as long as the strut body isn't weeping oil. This heuristic fails when applied to high-mileage Subarus like your 2004 Legacy (the "Bean"). While fluid leakage indicates seal failure, the absence of visible leaks does not guarantee structural integrity or proper damping characteristics. The fact that you upgraded from Capitol tires to Michelin MXV4s with negligible improvement in ride quality suggests the issue lies deeper within the suspension geometry or kinematics than simple rubber friction.

When diagnosing a harsh ride on an 88,000-mile vehicle, you must look beyond the shock absorber cylinder itself. The strut assembly is not merely a damper; it is a structural link that integrates the coil spring and often houses the top mount bearing. On older Subaru platforms, these top mounts are notorious wear points. If the internal bearings within the upper strut mount have seized or developed excessive play, the strut cannot pivot correctly during steering inputs. This results in a "clunking" sensation over bumps and a generally stiff, uncontrolled feel that mimics a suspension with completely failed dampers. The oil seal might be intact, but the mechanical connection to the chassis is likely compromised.

Furthermore, consider the condition of the lower strut mount and the bushings at the bottom of the shock tower. Rubber components degrade over time due to heat cycles and road salt exposure. When these rubber isolators harden or crack, they lose their ability to filter out high-frequency vibrations from the wheel travel. You feel every small imperfection in the road surface because the suspension is transmitting that energy directly to the cabin rather than absorbing it. This hardening effect becomes particularly pronounced when the tires are new and have a compliant sidewall, as the Michelin MXV4s confirmed by your testing. A stiff tire on a worn suspension highlights the chassis noise; a worn tire on a good suspension masks it.

Another critical factor to investigate is the sway bar (stabilizer bar) links and bushings. These components handle the lateral forces during cornering, but they also play a significant role in ride quality when the road surface is uneven. If the bushings have cracked or the ball joints are worn, the suspension will not articulate smoothly. The strut assembly alone cannot compensate for sloppy geometry elsewhere in the chassis.

To verify the diagnosis without disassembly immediately, perform a controlled compression test. Have an assistant sit in the passenger seat while you push down firmly on one corner of the vehicle. Release and observe how the car rebounds. If the vehicle bounces more than once or twice before settling, the damping is insufficient regardless of whether oil has leaked out. However, if the rebound feels stiff but controlled, the issue may be entirely mechanical play in the mounts rather than fluid loss.

Replacing the struts on a Subaru often requires replacing the entire assembly, including the top mount and lower bushings, to restore factory ride characteristics. Attempting to reuse old mounts on new struts is a common mistake that leads to recurring noise and harshness. The cost of labor for removing the strut towers can be significant, so ensure the decision to replace is based on a thorough inspection of all associated mounting points, not just the presence of leaking oil. If your vehicle continues to ride poorly after addressing these mechanical linkages, you will have confirmed whether the "Bean" inherently has a softer ride due to its original suspension tuning or if mechanical failure is the sole culprit.
